title: Hypothyroidism: Use TSH Correctly, Then Dose Levothyroxine to the Clinical Context
bottomLine: For suspected primary hypothyroidism, TSH is the preferred initial test and an abnormal TSH is interpreted with free T4. Central hypothyroidism is different: TSH may be normal or low despite low free T4, so dose monitoring relies on free T4 and pituitary context rather than TSH alone.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, menstrual change, bradycardia and cognitive slowing are common but nonspecific.
Pregnancy, amiodarone/lithium exposure and pituitary disease change testing and treatment context.
differentiate: High TSH plus low free T4 supports overt primary hypothyroidism; mild isolated TSH elevation requires context and repeat/etiology assessment rather than automatic high-dose treatment.
Low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH raises central hypothyroidism and possible broader pituitary disease.
assessment: Review symptoms, pregnancy/planning pregnancy, coronary disease/frailty, adherence, levothyroxine timing, iron/calcium/antacid interactions and prior thyroid surgery/radiation.
Look for pituitary symptoms or adrenal insufficiency clues before treating suspected central disease.
workup: Use TSH first for most primary disease and add free T4 appropriately; TPO antibodies can establish autoimmune etiology when that changes counselling but are not serial disease-activity tests.
In central disease, evaluate the pituitary axis and adrenal status before assuming routine primary hypothyroidism.
management: Use levothyroxine and individualize starting dose to age, cardiac disease, severity and pregnancy status.
Titrate primary disease using TSH after sufficient time for steady state; central disease is followed with free T4/clinical status through the pituitary plan.
medicationSafety: Iron, calcium and selected medications/foods impair levothyroxine absorption; consistency matters.
Over-replacement increases AF and bone risk; under-replacement can persist when adherence/timing is not addressed.
If central hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency are both possible, adrenal evaluation/treatment precedes thyroid hormone escalation to avoid precipitating crisis.
counselling: Teach consistent dosing and separation from interfering supplements; explain why symptom improvement and TSH normalization take time.
followUp: Recheck after clinically meaningful dose changes and more promptly in pregnancy; reassess adherence/timing before repeated dose escalation.
examTrap: Titrating suspected central hypothyroidism to TSH or increasing levothyroxine before considering coexisting adrenal insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: Primary hypothyroidism follows TSH; central hypothyroidism follows free T4 and the pituitary context.
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — Indications and Appropriate Use

title: Hyperthyroidism: Confirm Thyrotoxicosis, Then Identify Why It Is Happening
bottomLine: Suppressed TSH with elevated free thyroid hormone confirms biochemical thyrotoxicosis in the usual primary setting, but treatment depends on cause. Graves/toxic nodular overproduction, thyroiditis and exogenous hormone do not respond to the same therapy, and thyroid storm is a systemic emergency rather than simply a very low TSH.
recognize: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, AF, frequent stools and proximal weakness are common; older adults may present with AF, HF or apathy.
Graves can include diffuse goitre and thyroid-eye disease.
differentiate: Thyroiditis releases preformed hormone and generally does not respond to antithyroid drugs the way Graves/toxic nodular disease does.
Biotin/assay interference, pregnancy physiology and acute illness can distort thyroid tests.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, HF, eye symptoms, neck/nodule findings, pregnancy, iodine/amiodarone exposure, exogenous hormone and precipitating illness.
Ask fever/sore throat or hepatic symptoms if antithyroid medication is already used.
workup: Use TSH with free T4 and free T3 selectively when TSH is suppressed but free T4 does not explain suspected hyperthyroidism.
Use TRAb and imaging/uptake only when the etiologic question requires it and pregnancy/status permit.
management: Treat by cause: symptom control plus antithyroid medication, radioiodine or surgery for appropriate overproduction syndromes; supportive/anti-inflammatory treatment for thyroiditis when indicated.
Thyroid storm requires emergency multidrug/precipitant management in hospital.
medicationSafety: Methimazole/PTU can cause agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity; significant fever/sore throat or hepatic symptoms require urgent assessment.
Pregnancy changes antithyroid drug and definitive-treatment choices.
counselling: Teach medication-toxicity warning signs and smoking cessation in thyroid-eye disease.
followUp: Trend thyroid hormones and TSH according to treatment phase; ensure definitive/long-term plan when relapse risk remains.
examTrap: Escalating antithyroid medication for thyroiditis or calling a suppressed TSH alone thyroid storm.
oneLinePearl: Thyrotoxicosis is the biochemical state; the cause tells you the treatment.
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — Indications and Appropriate Use

title: Thyroid Nodule: TSH and Ultrasound Risk Before FNA
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule needs clinical risk assessment, TSH and risk-stratified ultrasound. FNA is based on sonographic pattern plus size/clinical risk—not palpability, anxiety or size alone—and a suppressed TSH can change the pathway toward functional assessment before biopsy.
recognize: Rapid growth, hard/fixed lesion, cervical nodes, hoarseness, radiation exposure and strong familial thyroid-cancer syndromes increase concern.
Most incidentally detected thyroid nodules are benign.
differentiate: A hyperfunctioning nodule has a different malignancy/workup pathway from a nonfunctioning suspicious nodule.
Thyroglobulin is not a general screening test for malignancy in a patient with an intact thyroid.
assessment: Assess compressive symptoms, voice change, thyroid symptoms, radiation/family history and cervical nodes.
Review prior ultrasound and growth rather than treating every small measurement change as true progression.
workup: Order TSH and high-quality thyroid ultrasound; use current risk classification to decide FNA.
Use functional imaging when indicated by suppressed TSH, not routinely for every euthyroid nodule.
management: Refer nodules with suspicious cytology/imaging, significant compression or high-risk clinical features.
Use surveillance rather than immediate biopsy/surgery for nodules below evidence-based FNA thresholds.
medicationSafety: Do not use routine levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules because harms can exceed benefit.
counselling: Explain that not every nodule needs biopsy and that ultrasound-risk pattern guides safe surveillance.
followUp: Use risk/cytology-specific ultrasound follow-up and close the loop on biopsy results.
examTrap: Biopsying every incidental thyroid nodule or ordering thyroglobulin to screen an intact thyroid for cancer.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-nodule biopsy is ultrasound-risk driven, not fear driven.
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — Indications and Appropriate Use

title: Differentiated Thyroid Cancer Follow-Up: Risk-Adapt Surveillance to Treatment and Response
bottomLine: Thyroid-cancer surveillance is risk- and response-adapted. After differentiated thyroid-cancer treatment, interpret thyroglobulin together with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, TSH targets, ultrasound and the patient's treatment history; do not treat one detectable tumor-marker value as recurrence without context.
recognize: Thyroglobulin is useful after treatment for papillary/follicular differentiated thyroid cancer because it can function as a tumor marker in the appropriate post-treatment setting.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies can make thyroglobulin results unreliable and must be interpreted concurrently.
differentiate: Thyroglobulin in a patient with an intact untreated thyroid is not a useful generic cancer screening test.
Surveillance intensity differs by original recurrence risk and response to therapy rather than a single fixed schedule for everyone.
assessment: Review pathology/stage, surgery extent, radioiodine history, prior Tg/anti-Tg/ultrasound trends, TSH suppression target, pregnancy plans and symptoms/nodal findings.
workup: Use thyroglobulin plus anti-Tg, neck ultrasound and additional imaging according to risk/response and endocrinology/oncology plan.
Trend results using comparable assays/conditions where feasible rather than reacting to tiny isolated changes.
management: Maintain individualized TSH target and specialist follow-up based on recurrence risk and treatment response.
Escalate rising biochemical/structural evidence to endocrinology/thyroid-oncology rather than reflexively intensifying levothyroxine.
medicationSafety: Excessive chronic TSH suppression can increase AF and bone risk, especially in older adults; suppression target should reflect cancer risk and response.
redFlags: Progressive rising tumor marker with reliable assay
counselling: Explain that recurrence surveillance uses trends and imaging together and that TSH suppression intensity may change over time.
followUp: Maintain closed-loop specialist surveillance and ensure pending imaging/tumor-marker trends are reviewed.
examTrap: Calling any detectable thyroglobulin recurrent cancer without checking residual thyroid tissue, anti-Tg antibodies, assay context and trend.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-cancer surveillance is marker + antibody + imaging + risk—not one number.

title: Adrenal Insufficiency: Prove Cortisol Deficiency, But Treat Crisis Before the Test Is Perfect
bottomLine: Stable suspected adrenal insufficiency requires appropriately timed cortisol/ACTH-based evaluation and cause classification; adrenal crisis is different and requires immediate glucocorticoid plus fluid/resuscitation treatment without waiting for confirmatory testing.
recognize: Fatigue, weight loss, nausea, postural symptoms, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia are nonspecific; hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation support primary disease.
Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can suppress the HPA axis and abrupt withdrawal can precipitate crisis.
differentiate: Primary adrenal insufficiency can impair both cortisol and aldosterone; central disease generally preserves mineralocorticoid function.
A random cortisol during stable outpatient evaluation may be difficult to interpret; timing and clinical context matter.
assessment: Review all systemic/inhaled/injected/topical steroid exposure, autoimmune disease, pituitary symptoms, infection, pregnancy and medication interactions.
In suspected crisis assess shock, vomiting, mental status, glucose and electrolytes immediately.
workup: Use morning cortisol/ACTH and stimulation testing when indicated in stable patients, plus renin/aldosterone for primary disease where appropriate.
During crisis draw cortisol/ACTH if feasible before therapy only if this does not delay treatment.
management: Replace glucocorticoid physiologically in confirmed chronic disease and add mineralocorticoid replacement for primary aldosterone deficiency when indicated.
Adrenal crisis requires emergency parenteral glucocorticoid, isotonic fluids, glucose/electrolyte support and treatment of the precipitant.
medicationSafety: Never abruptly stop prolonged systemic glucocorticoids when HPA suppression is plausible.
Patients need sick-day/stress-dose plans and emergency injectable steroid access when appropriate.
counselling: Teach steroid card/medical alert, sick-day rules, emergency injection and when to seek emergency care.
followUp: Review replacement adequacy, BP/electrolytes and crisis prevention; reassess HPA recovery after exogenous-steroid taper when appropriate.
examTrap: Waiting for an ACTH stimulation test before treating shock in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: Stable adrenal insufficiency is a diagnostic pathway; adrenal crisis is a treat-now pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism practice resources

title: Cushing Syndrome: First Exclude Steroid Exposure, Then Screen the Right Phenotype
bottomLine: Do not screen everyone with obesity, diabetes or hypertension for Cushing syndrome. Test when multiple progressive/discriminatory features make hypercortisolism plausible, and first identify exogenous glucocorticoid exposure; abnormal screening tests establish hypercortisolism probability before localization—not the adrenal or pituitary source.
recognize: Easy bruising, proximal weakness, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, osteoporosis, growth deceleration in children and difficult hypertension/diabetes are more discriminatory than obesity alone.
Exogenous steroid exposure is the most important mimic/cause to identify before endocrine testing.
differentiate: Alcohol use, severe depression, uncontrolled diabetes and other pseudo-Cushing states can alter cortisol physiology.
ACTH/localization testing comes after biochemical hypercortisolism is established.
assessment: Review oral, inhaled, injected, topical and nonprescription/supplement steroid exposure.
Assess thromboembolism, infection, bone, glucose/BP, psychiatric and reproductive complications.
workup: Use validated first-line cortisol screening tests chosen to the patient/context and confirm abnormal results appropriately.
Avoid random cortisol or imaging as the first diagnostic step in stable suspected Cushing syndrome.
management: Refer confirmed endogenous hypercortisolism for endocrine localization and definitive treatment.
Taper exogenous steroids safely when feasible; do not abruptly stop chronic therapy.
medicationSafety: Cortisol-lowering therapy is specialist-managed and can cause adrenal insufficiency/interactions.
Thrombotic/infection risk can be substantial in active severe Cushing syndrome.
counselling: Explain why confirmatory hormone testing precedes scanning and why steroid exposure from any route matters.
followUp: Monitor cardiovascular, metabolic, bone and infection complications while definitive endocrine care proceeds.
examTrap: Ordering adrenal CT because obesity and hypertension 'look Cushingoid' before confirming hypercortisolism and excluding exogenous steroids.
oneLinePearl: Cushing workup goes phenotype → biochemical proof → source localization.
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — Indications and Appropriate Use

title: Pheochromocytoma: Biochemical Proof Before Tumour Localization
bottomLine: Suspect pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma with a compatible episodic catecholamine syndrome, adrenal mass or hereditary-risk context. Use plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrine testing under appropriate collection conditions before localization imaging; once confirmed, preoperative alpha-blockade/volume strategy is specialist-led and beta blockade never precedes adequate alpha blockade.
recognize: Episodic headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, labile/paroxysmal hypertension, pallor/tremor or panic-like spells can occur.
An adrenal incidentaloma or hereditary syndrome can prompt evaluation even without the classic triad.
differentiate: Panic disorder, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, stimulant use and medication withdrawal can mimic adrenergic spells.
Plasma catecholamines are not the preferred screening test; metanephrines provide better biochemical assessment.
assessment: Review spell timing/triggers, BP pattern, family/genetic history, adrenal imaging, medications/substances and pregnancy.
Assess cardiovascular complications and crisis features.
workup: Use plasma free metanephrines or urinary fractionated metanephrines according to access/pretest probability and collection requirements.
Localize with CT/MRI only after biochemical evidence, except selected urgent/incidental contexts coordinated with specialists.
management: Refer confirmed disease for endocrine/genetic/surgical management.
Preoperative preparation uses alpha blockade and volume expansion; add beta blockade only after adequate alpha blockade when tachycardia requires it.
medicationSafety: Beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade can cause unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction and severe hypertensive crisis.
Many drugs/collection conditions can cause false-positive biochemical results and need review.
counselling: Explain why biochemical confirmation comes before tumour hunting and why hereditary assessment may involve relatives.
followUp: Ensure endocrine/genetic/surgical follow-up and postoperative biochemical surveillance are closed-loop.
examTrap: Starting a beta blocker for pheochromocytoma tachycardia before alpha blockade or ordering adrenal imaging before biochemical confirmation in a stable patient.
oneLinePearl: Pheochromocytoma: prove catecholamine excess first; alpha before beta.
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — plasma free metanephrines

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Confirm Calcium Physiology Before Calling the Gland Abnormal
bottomLine: Primary hyperparathyroidism is diagnosed biochemically: elevated calcium with an inappropriately elevated or nonsuppressed PTH after confirming calcium status and excluding important mimics/secondary causes. Parathyroid imaging localizes surgery; it does not diagnose the disease.
recognize: Patients may be asymptomatic or have nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis/fracture, constipation, neurocognitive symptoms or renal impairment.
Medication effects such as thiazides/lithium and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can mimic parts of the pattern.
differentiate: Secondary hyperparathyroidism usually occurs with low/normal calcium from vitamin-D deficiency, CKD or malabsorption.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia should be considered when urinary calcium is unexpectedly low and family history/context fit.
assessment: Review stones, fractures/BMD, kidney disease, medications, calcium/vitamin-D intake and family history.
Assess dehydration or neuro/cardiac symptoms if calcium is substantially elevated.
workup: Confirm corrected/ionized calcium as appropriate and measure PTH, creatinine/eGFR, phosphate, vitamin D and urinary calcium according to the diagnostic question.
Use DEXA/renal imaging as indicated for complication assessment; use parathyroid imaging only after diagnosis when surgery is planned.
management: Refer patients meeting surgical/complication criteria for endocrine/surgical evaluation and parathyroidectomy consideration.
When managed nonoperatively, monitor calcium, renal and skeletal outcomes and correct avoidable vitamin-D deficiency carefully.
medicationSafety: Avoid excessive calcium/vitamin-D loading during significant hypercalcemia without a defined plan.
Review thiazide/lithium contribution but do not stop essential therapy without context.
counselling: Explain that the diagnosis comes from hormone-calcium physiology; the scan is for surgical planning.
followUp: Track calcium, kidney function, stone/skeletal risk and operative criteria.
examTrap: Ordering a sestamibi scan to diagnose hyperparathyroidism before confirming the calcium/PTH pattern.
oneLinePearl: Parathyroid imaging finds the gland after biochemistry proves the disease.

title: Hypoparathyroidism: Replace Calcium Carefully and Protect the Kidney
bottomLine: Chronic hypoparathyroidism causes low calcium with absent/inappropriately low PTH and often high phosphate. Treat symptoms and maintain calcium in a safe individualized range with calcium/active vitamin-D therapy while avoiding hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis and renal injury; acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is a monitored IV-calcium emergency.
recognize: Perioral/finger paresthesias, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation can occur with significant hypocalcemia.
Postsurgical neck history is common, but autoimmune/genetic and infiltrative causes also occur.
differentiate: Vitamin-D deficiency and CKD can produce hypocalcemia with secondary high PTH rather than hypoparathyroidism.
Hypomagnesemia can cause functional PTH deficiency/resistance and must be corrected.
assessment: Assess symptoms, neck surgery/radiation, medications, magnesium, renal history, pregnancy and adherence to calcium/calcitriol.
workup: Confirm calcium (corrected/ionized where appropriate), PTH, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR and urinary calcium according to chronic management needs.
management: Use oral calcium plus active vitamin-D therapy individualized to symptoms/serum and urine calcium.
Treat severe symptomatic hypocalcemia with monitored IV calcium and correct magnesium.
Refer difficult control, renal complications or pregnancy to endocrinology.
medicationSafety: Over-replacement can cause hypercalciuria, stones and nephrocalcinosis even when serum calcium appears acceptable.
Thiazides may be used selectively for hypercalciuria under a monitored plan.
counselling: Teach consistent dosing and symptoms of both low and high calcium; avoid unsupervised dose escalation.
followUp: Monitor serum calcium/phosphate/magnesium/renal function and urinary calcium at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Chasing a high-normal serum calcium in chronic hypoparathyroidism and causing hypercalciuria/renal damage.
oneLinePearl: Hypoparathyroidism treatment balances symptoms and serum calcium against kidney calcium exposure.

title: Vitamin D: Test When Risk Changes Care, Supplement to Need—not Megadose by Reflex
bottomLine: Vitamin-D testing and supplementation should answer a clinical bone/mineral question. Routine population testing and indiscriminate high-dose supplementation are low value; test and replace when deficiency risk, malabsorption, osteoporosis therapy or calcium/PTH abnormalities make the result actionable, then avoid chronic excessive dosing.
recognize: Deficiency risk rises with malabsorption, limited intake/sun exposure, some medications, CKD/liver disease and selected bone/mineral disorders.
Severe deficiency can contribute to osteomalacia, muscle weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
differentiate: Vitamin-D supplementation in generally healthy adults should not be marketed as a stand-alone fracture/fall prevention strategy.
A low vitamin-D value must be interpreted with calcium, phosphate, PTH, kidney/liver and clinical context when bone/mineral disease is present.
assessment: Assess dietary intake, supplements, malabsorption, fracture/osteoporosis risk, medications and conditions affecting vitamin-D metabolism.
Document actual supplement dose before prescribing more.
workup: Order 25-hydroxyvitamin D when the result will change management—such as high deficiency risk, selected osteoporosis/mineral disorders or malabsorption—not as indiscriminate screening.
Use calcium/PTH/phosphate and other tests when the clinical syndrome requires them.
management: Use Health Canada/Osteoporosis Canada dietary/supplement guidance and individualized replacement for confirmed deficiency/risk.
Ensure adequate calcium/vitamin-D status when initiating osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, while prioritizing effective osteoporosis drugs for high fracture risk rather than supplements alone.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated high-dose bolus or chronic excessive vitamin D because hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and other harms can occur.
Granulomatous disease and selected endocrine/renal disorders require caution with supplementation.
redFlags: Bone pain/fracture with suspected mineralization disorder
counselling: Explain that vitamin D supports bone/mineral health but is not a substitute for indicated osteoporosis therapy or balanced nutrition/activity.
followUp: Repeat levels only when the result can guide a high-risk replacement/absorption plan rather than routinely after every supplement change.
examTrap: Ordering vitamin-D levels on every healthy adult or prescribing megadose vitamin D as the main fracture-prevention treatment in a high-risk osteoporosis patient.
oneLinePearl: Test vitamin D when it changes care; treat deficiency without turning supplementation into the whole bone plan.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada July 2026 Vitamin D and Calcium Evidence Update
